events.title: The Edict of Milan grants toleration to Christians
events.shortBlurb: The emperors Constantine and Licinius agreed to grant Christians freedom of worship, ending the age of persecution in the Roman Empire…
body: In February 313 the emperors Constantine and Licinius met at Milan, where Licinius married Constantine's half-sister Constantia, and agreed on a common policy of religious freedom for the empire. Their decision, remembered as the Edict of Milan, survives not as a single decree but as a letter of Licinius to the eastern governors, posted at Nicomedia on 13 June 313 and preserved by the Christian writers Lactantius and Eusebius.

The letter granted to Christians, and indeed to all men, the free power to follow the religion of their choice, and it ordered that the churches, cemeteries, and other property seized in the persecutions be restored to the Christian communities without payment. In this it went beyond the edict of the dying Galerius in 311, which had merely permitted Christians to exist.

The agreement marked the decisive turn from persecution to the peace of the Church. Constantine, victor over his rival Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge the previous October, ruled the whole empire alone by 324, and by the end of the century Christianity had passed from a proscribed sect to the favored faith of the Roman state.
